questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion resting on a premise nobody stated
questions.learningObjective: Identify a conclusion with an unstated premise
questions.stem: A club argues the event failed because members were disengaged, though engagement was never measured; what is wrong?

options.text: The conclusion rests on a premise nobody stated

questions.explanation: The conclusion assumes an unstated premise about engagement. The tempting wrong idea flips the verdict or denies measurement.
questions.hint: Ask where engagement was established.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion the premises reach too far to support
questions.learningObjective: Spot a conclusion that overreaches its premises
questions.stem: From 'five members improved' a club concludes 'the programme is proven'; what is wrong?
questions.explanation: The conclusion overreaches from five members to proof. The tempting wrong idea flips the verdict or overstates the sample.
questions.hint: Check the scope of the premise against the conclusion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion about the future drawn from two facts about the present
questions.learningObjective: Identify an unsupported future projection
questions.stem: A club concludes next season will thrive because current sponsorship is strong and facilities are new; what is wrong?

options.text: Sponsorship is not a good measure
It projects the future from two present facts

questions.explanation: Two present facts do not support a future conclusion. The tempting wrong idea attacks a premise or flips the projection.
questions.hint: Check whether time is bridged by evidence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with a false conclusion
questions.learningObjective: Recognise validity with a false conclusion
questions.stem: A club argument is valid but one premise is false; what follows about the conclusion?

answer.exemplar: The conclusion may be false, because validity preserves truth but a false premise can yield a false conclusion.

questions.explanation: A false premise can yield a false conclusion. The tempting wrong idea equates validity with truth.
questions.hint: Validity is about form, not content.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A valid argument with true premises
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a valid argument with true premises

stimulus.body: A club argument is valid and all premises are true. The conclusion follows necessarily.

questions.stem: What follows?

options.text: The conclusion may still be false

questions.explanation: Validity plus true premises guarantees a true conclusion. The tempting wrong idea doubts the guarantee.
questions.hint: That is the definition of soundness.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A passage that persuades without arguing
questions.learningObjective: Identify persuasion without argument
questions.stem: A club newsletter praises the committee in warm language and lists achievements but offers no reasons; what does it do?
questions.explanation: Praise and listing can persuade without argument. The tempting wrong idea assumes hidden premises.
questions.hint: Look for reasons, not just positive language.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A counterexample that does not refute
questions.learningObjective: Identify a counterexample that fails to refute
questions.stem: A club claims training helps most members; one member did not improve; does this refute?

answer.exemplar: No, a single case does not refute a majority claim, because one exception is compatible with most members benefiting.

questions.explanation: One case does not refute a majority claim. The tempting wrong idea treats any counterexample as decisive.
questions.hint: Check whether the claim is universal or general.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A claim no result could count against
questions.learningObjective: Identify an unfalsifiable claim

stimulus.body: A club claims its spirit is 'unmeasurable but decisive'. Any outcome is interpreted as consistent with this spirit.

questions.stem: Why can no result count against it?

options.text: The claim is unfalsifiable and absorbs any result

questions.explanation: An unmeasurable claim absorbs any result. The tempting wrong idea denies the premise or assumes bad faith.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence would disprove it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A summary that leaves out the detail qualifying it
questions.learningObjective: Spot a summary that drops a qualifier
questions.stem: A club summary states 'the plan works' for a study that concluded 'the plan works for novices only'; what is wrong?

options.text: It leaves out the detail qualifying it

questions.explanation: Omitting the qualifier overgeneralises. The tempting wrong idea blames length or attacks the source.
questions.hint: Check what qualifier disappeared.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A citation that supports a weaker claim than the one made
questions.learningObjective: Identify a citation supporting a weaker claim

stimulus.body: A club cites a study showing 'some benefit' to support 'major improvement'. The study's wording is milder than the report's.

questions.stem: What is the mismatch?

options.text: The citation supports a weaker claim than the one made

questions.explanation: The citation supports a weaker claim than asserted. The tempting wrong idea assumes fabrication or normalises overclaiming.
questions.hint: Compare the strength of the two claims.
